hook: You know “Be strong and courageous”. But did you know God says it to Joshua three times in a single chapter?
story:
The book of Joshua opens with a death: “Moses my servant is dead.” Now the people stood at the edge of the Jordan River without him.

Joshua was not a stranger to the work. The Jewish Virtual Library says he first appears in Exodus 17, under the name Hosea, and that he was one of the twelve men sent to scout the land. The page adds that of that generation, only he and Caleb survived. When Moses neared his death, the same page says, Joshua was chosen to be his successor.

Then God speaks to him, and the command comes in waves. In verse 6: “Be strong and courageous”. In verse 7: “Only be strong and very courageous”. And in our verse, the third time, it comes as a question and a promise together: “Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”

The text does not tell us what Joshua felt. It tells us what God said, and what Joshua did next: he commanded the officers of the people. The people answered him: “Just as we listened to Moses in all things, so will we listen to you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses.” And they ended with the words God had used: “Only be strong and courageous.”

moment:
Just before our verse, God has laid out the task: cross this Jordan, take the land, and keep the book of the law close, so that “you shall meditate on it day and night”.

Then comes verse 9. It sits between a long list of instructions and the first order Joshua gives to his own people. It is the hinge of the chapter: what God has said to him becomes what he says to them.
around: Before the verse, God promises: “No man will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you nor forsake you.” After it, Joshua commands the officers: “Pass through the middle of the camp, and command the people”.
after:
The promise was tested within days. At the Jordan, God told Joshua, “Today I will begin to magnify you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.” When the priests carrying the ark stepped into the river, the water upstream stood in a heap, and “all Israel crossed over on dry ground”. From that day, the text says, the people held Joshua in awe as they had held Moses, all his life.

Courage did not mean that nothing went wrong. At Ai, a town the spies said had only a few defenders, Israel’s men ran, and about thirty-six of them were killed. “The hearts of the people melted, and became like water.” Joshua tore his clothes and lay on his face before the ark until evening, with dust on his head, and cried out, “I wish that we had been content and lived beyond the Jordan!” God answered, “Get up!”, named the theft hidden in the camp that lay behind the defeat, and then spoke to him in almost the words of the first chapter: “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed.”

In time Joshua was the one passing the words on. After another battle he told his commanders, “Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed. Be strong and courageous”.

Old and near death, he gathered all Israel and told them that “not one thing has failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spoke concerning you.” Then he made his own choice in front of them: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” He died at one hundred ten. Israel served the LORD as long as Joshua and the elders who outlived him were alive. Then, the book of Judges says, another generation arose “who didn’t know the LORD”. The courage of one generation did not pass to the next by itself.
readings:
Many readers hear this verse as a personal word of comfort, for any frightening road. They hear God promising to be present wherever they go, and they take it with them.

Read inside the chapter, it is first a charge to one leader at a turning point in the story of a nation, and the people take it up together at the end. The two readings are not rivals. The words were given to a person with a task, and believers have carried them into their own tasks ever since.

On either reading the courage is not self-confidence. Verse 9 gives its reason in the same breath as the command: “for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”
argued:
Commentators have long noticed where the weight of this verse rests. The English commentator Matthew Henry wrote: [[henry]]

John Gill asked readers to think about who gives the order, and judged that the promise of God was enough: [[gill]]

A modern preacher, Erin M. Stout, notes the same pattern of the command growing stronger each time and what it asked of Joshua: [[stout]]

Three writers, one steady point: the courage is asked for, and the reason for it is given with it.
point: God does not tell Joshua to feel brave. He tells him, three times in one chapter, to be strong, and in verse 9 he gives the reason: the LORD is with him wherever he goes.
lesson:
Maybe you are standing at your own river: a new job, a hard diagnosis, a child to raise alone, a role someone else filled before you. Joshua knew that place. Moses was dead, the people were waiting, and the work was his.

Look at what God gave him. Not a guarantee that every day would go well: Ai came soon after Jericho, and Joshua ended up face down in the dust. Not a speech about believing in himself. He was given a task, a book to keep close day and night, and a presence that would go with him wherever he went.

So begin where Joshua was told to begin. Open the word and stay with it. Ask God for help with the next step, not the whole road, and take that step. If you end up on your face, as Joshua did, remember that God’s first words to him there were about getting up, and about dealing honestly with what had gone wrong.

Later Joshua was the one telling others, “Be strong and courageous”. Someone near you may need to hear it from you.

If you do not share this faith, the story still says something true about people: courage comes more easily to someone who knows they are not facing the task alone.

echoes.note: Before he died, Moses had already said it to Joshua in front of all Israel: “The LORD himself is who goes before you. He will be with you.” Joshua 1 confirms what Joshua had heard from Moses.

Generations later David handed a great work, the building of the temple, to his young son Solomon with the same words: “Be strong and courageous, and do it.” Again the reason is a presence, not a plan.
Through Isaiah, God tells his people again and again not to be afraid, and gives the reason Joshua was given: “Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you.”

The letter to the Hebrews gives the promise of Joshua 1:5 to ordinary believers, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you”, and draws the same conclusion: “with good courage we say”.
